fields.description: Every revival is born in prayer. Here is how to pray for revival — united, persistent, honest, and God-centred — and to keep praying until he comes.
fields.body_html:
If you long to see God move in power — to see a cold church come awake, a hard family softened, a nation turned back to Christ — the first and last work is prayer. Every revival worthy of the name has been born in it, sustained by it, and traced back to it when its history is honestly written. Revival is God’s to give; but he has bound himself to give it to a people who ask. So the practical question is not whether to pray for revival, but how. How do you pray so that heaven opens?

Scripture and the record of every awakening answer with a remarkable consistency. The prayer that seeks revival is united, persistent, honest, and God-centred. It is less about eloquence than about desperation. This is not a technique for forcing God’s hand — he will not be manipulated — but the very hunger through which he prepares to answer. Here is how to pray for revival, and to keep praying until it comes.

Begin where every revival has begun — on your knees together

Before the Spirit fell at Pentecost, the church was doing one thing: praying. Luke records that the disciples “with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer” (Acts 1:14). For ten days a small, frightened band gave itself to united intercession, and then the wind and fire came. That order is not accidental; it is the pattern of the whole book. When the church prayed again in Acts 4, “the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31).

Notice the word together. Revival prayer is rarely the work of a lone hero; it is a people crying out with one accord. The great awakenings of history were cradled in prayer meetings — often small, often obscure, often for years before anything visible stirred. The point is not the size of the gathering but its unity and its earnestness. If you would pray for revival, do not pray only in your closet, precious as that is. Find two or three others who are hungry, and give yourselves to seeking God together. Heaven has a particular affection for the agreement of a praying people (Matthew 18:19–20). What God did through a hundred and twenty in an upper room, he can do through the few he finds gathered and asking.

Pray for a spirit of grace and supplication

There is a mystery at the heart of revival prayer: the desire to pray for revival is itself a gift of God. Before he pours out the blessing, he pours out the burden. Zechariah foresaw the day when God would “pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy” (Zechariah 12:10) — and the mourning and turning that followed. The very ache to see God move, the holy dissatisfaction with a comfortable, powerless Christianity, is the first drop of the coming rain.

So do not despise small beginnings in your own heart. If you find yourself grieved by the deadness around you and hungry for more of God, that grief is not from yourself — it is the Spirit setting a fire that he means to spread. Ask God for more of it. Pray, “Lord, give us the spirit of prayer; make us groan for what you long to give.” A church that has lost even the desire to pray for revival should make that its first petition: that God would revive its praying before he revives anything else.

Be importunate — pray as though you will not be refused

Jesus told a whole parable to teach one thing about prayer: “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). The widow wore down an unjust judge by sheer refusal to give up; how much more, Jesus says, will the righteous God answer his elect “who cry to him day and night”? Revival prayer is importunate prayer. It does not ask once and file the request away; it lays hold of God and will not let go.

Isaiah pictures such praying as a night watch that never falls silent: “On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have set watchmen; all the day and all the night they shall never be silent. You who put the Lord in remembrance, take no rest, and give him no rest until he establishes Jerusalem and makes it a praise in the earth” (Isaiah 62:6–7). To give God no rest — that is the boldness Scripture invites. It is not irreverence; it is faith taking his promises seriously enough to plead them back to him. The prayer that changed nations was seldom polite and occasional. It was the cry of people who had decided they would rather die than go on as they were.

Men are God’s method. The Church is looking for better methods; God is looking for better men.E. M. Bounds

Bounds, who wrote more searchingly on prayer than almost anyone, understood that God works through praying people more than through polished programs. The engine of every awakening is not machinery but intercession, and the intercessors God uses are simply ordinary believers who refuse to stop asking.

Pray with confession, not just petition

Revival prayer is honest about sin — its own first of all. The prophets who pleaded for their people did not pray as spectators of others’ failings; they confessed as members of a guilty community. Daniel prayed, “we have sinned and done wrong.” When James promises that “the prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working” and points to Elijah, who prayed and the heavens gave rain, he sets it beside a command: “confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16–18). The rain of revival tends to fall on ground first broken by repentance.

So let your praying for revival include unhurried, specific confession — of coldness, of prayerlessness, of the sins the church has learned to tolerate. Do not rush past this to the exciting part. It is the exciting part, for God “dwells with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly” (Isaiah 57:15). A people willing to be searched is a people ready to be visited.

Ask God himself to come down

Above all, revival prayer asks for God — not merely for results, blessings, or numbers, but for his manifest presence. The great revival prayer of Isaiah is naked longing: “Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence” (Isaiah 64:1). And the Psalmist cries, “Turn again, O God of hosts! Look down from heaven, and see... Then we shall not turn back from you; give us life, and we will call upon your name. Restore us, O Lord God of hosts! Let your face shine, that we may be saved” (Psalm 80:14, 18–19).

This is the deepest note of all. Revival is not a program we run or an atmosphere we generate; it is God drawing near to a people until they cannot mistake his presence. Ask for that. Ask him to come down. And remember the staggering encouragement Jesus attached to such asking: the Father gives “the Holy Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke 11:13). If revival is, at bottom, the Spirit poured out, then Jesus has told us plainly how to seek it — ask, and keep asking, for the Spirit.

Pray specifically, and expect God to answer

Vague prayer expects little and receives little. Revival prayer, by contrast, is bold and definite — it names what it asks and looks for the answer. God’s own invitation is astonishing in its openness: “Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known” (Jeremiah 33:3). He does not merely tolerate our asking; he invites it, and promises to show us things beyond our imagining. Jesus pressed the same confidence: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives” (Matthew 7:7–8).

So pray specifically for your own church, your own town, your own family and friends by name. Ask God to save particular people, to soften particular hardness, to pour out his Spirit in a particular place. And then watch for the answer with expectant faith, for “whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours” (Mark 11:24). Faith does not mean certainty about the timing; God often waits, and part of importunate prayer is trusting his wisdom about when. But it does mean praying as though the God who promised is real and listening — because he is. Keep a record, if it helps, of what you are asking, and let each answered prayer become fresh fuel for the next. A praying people who expect nothing will pray listlessly; a praying people who expect God to move will pray until he does.

Stand in the gap, and do not give up

God once searched a whole nation for a single intercessor: “I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none” (Ezekiel 22:30). It is a sobering verse and a thrilling one — sobering because judgment came for want of one who would pray, thrilling because it shows how much God will do in answer to even one who will stand in the gap.

You may be that one. The praying grandmother, the small midweek group, the believer who rises early to plead for a sleeping church — these are the people through whom God has again and again begun his greatest works. Do not wait for a crowd, a platform, or a feeling. Begin. Gather whoever will come. Confess honestly, ask boldly, and refuse to stop until he answers. History and Scripture agree on this: God has never long withheld revival from a people who would humble themselves and pray, and he has never yet poured it out on a people who would not. So take him at his word, and give him no rest. Will you not stand in the gap and pray until he comes?
